title: Morning preview
tomorrow: a young man walks into a river at dawn and doesn't come out. then?

lines: THE EASY MEETING AND THE HARD ONE.
I SHALL MEET WITH THE BUSY-BODY.
cards: Your calendar already knows who you'll see today, the easy meeting and the hard one.

Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, kept a private notebook we now call the Meditations, and one entry opens like a warning to himself: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial."
An emperor, listing who's going to annoy him. Why start a day that way?

teach.h: THEY DON'T KNOW GOOD FROM EVIL.
teach.b: Because of what comes next: "All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil."
Marcus was a Stoic, and in the same entry he says none of them can injure him, because no one can drag him into what is ugly.

teach.h: NO ONE CAN HARM YOUR CHARACTER.
teach.b: For him, the only real harm is harm to his own character. So the rude person can't truly injure him. And he can't hate them either, because, he says, they are his kin, sharing in the same reason.
Then the picture: "For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth." That's the teaching: the Stoic morning preview.

You rehearse the hard people before you meet them, not to brace for a fight, but so you've already chosen how you'll act, as one hand working with another. Notice he doesn't pretend everyone will be pleasant.
He expects the difficult ones and decides on kindness in advance.
That's the line between a preview and a worry.
A worry rehearses the bad scene. A preview rehearses you, at your best, inside it.

how: Some readers of the Stoics practice the morning preview from Meditations 2.1: before the day starts, they picture the difficult people and moments ahead and decide how they want to meet them.

o: rehearsing the day's people and choosing how you'll meet them
checking the weather and the traffic before leaving home
reading a summary of the news before you get up

games.q: a week of mornings: tap the pairs.
p: prayer a great while before day
knowing each breath as it is
I shall meet with the busy-body

s: Marcus's preview is about expecting the worst from people
he expects difficult people but decides ahead not to hate them: we're made for cooperation.
Marcus writes that none of the difficult people can truly injure him
no one can drag him into what is ugly, so he's free to choose kindness.

games.q: your roommate has a tense talk with the landlord at noon and has replayed the fight in her head all morning. what would Marcus's preview change?
o: picture the talk and decide now how she'll act: calmly, kindly, like hand with hand.
rehearse every insult he might say so she has comebacks ready.
don't think about the landlord at all until noon arrives.
games.why: Marcus doesn't pretend the hard person away. he names them, remembers they're kin, and chooses how he'll act before the meeting.

practice: Walk through today in order, and stop at the person you're least looking forward to. Picture the moment you'll meet them, and picture yourself meeting them kindly, the way Marcus decided before his day began.
Then let the picture go and rest in a few slow breaths.

wordCard.voice: Morning preview: meeting the day's hard people in your mind first, and choosing kindness before you get there. The Stoic preview of Marcus Aurelius.

orig.note: Greek: working together. Marcus says we are made for it (Meditations 2.1).

carryVoice: Hold on to this: I'll meet them kindly, like hand with hand. A week of mornings, done.
